title: Many Iranians Forced to Take Out Loans to Pay for Daily Essentials
author: Fateme Karimkhan
content:

Iranian woman looks at fruit while shopping in the traditional Grand Bazaar in
southern Tehran, Iran, on September 1, 2026, amid rising tensions between Iran
and the United States. Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images.

A video that recently went viral on Iranian social media shows people [eating
caviar](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DctbnXmto81/) and rare salmon for
breakfast in Tehran, a meal costing around 10 million tomans ($50), the
monthly wage for many Iranians. Another viral video shows a man wrapping a
thick piece of red meat between two layers of bacon, adding additional meat,
and then wrapping the concoction in a bun soaked with fat.

Such videos have become increasingly popular in Iran as the country grapples
with the rising cost of meat and other food staples.

The head of Iran's Association of Meat and Protein Products Packing Industry
said in late May that in response to the high prices, demand for meat products
had fallen 50% compared with the previous year. Last summer, one kilogram of
mutton cost around 1 million tomans; this summer, the same portion reached 2
million tomans ($10).

The announcement of a new campaign of sanctions targeted against Iran on
August 24--dubbed Operation Economic Outcast by the U.S. Treasury Department--
and aimed at further turning the screws on the Iranian economy, has been met
with a shrug by many ordinary Iranians already exhausted from trying to
survive during a rapid collapse of living standards unseen in the country's
modern history.

The new campaign, which has so far included the sanctioning of several banks
and airlines servicing Iran, comes on top of a blockade of the country's
southern ports, which has halted the import of basic resources. As the
sanctions campaign continues, the Iranian rial has collapsed, falling
Wednesday to a record low of roughly 2.34 million rials to the dollar, making
already scarce imports dramatically more expensive.

Iranians have now been forced to navigate a situation in which obtaining the
bare necessities of life requires accepting potentially ruinous personal
debts, or is simply impossible.

"A packet of tea that used to cost 300,000 to 600,000 tomans [$2-4] now costs
one million tomans [$5] after the war. Why should a packet of tea cost one
million tomans when a worker's daily wage is not even one million tomans? If
you are a day laborer, you have to give up even buying tea," said a
construction worker in Tehran, who like others who spoke to Drop Site for this
article, requested anonymity to avoid retaliation. "Soap, dental floss,
tobacco, and goods like these have become unaffordable for us. Our situation
has become embarrassing. To buy the personal hygiene products we actually
want, we have to take out loans."

## Food and Medicine

While the Iranian government initially sought to cushion the economic crisis
at the start of the year by
[providing](https://english.aawsat.com/world/5226275-iranians-receive-monthly-
payment-amid-economic-woes-protests) approximately 80 million people with
monthly electronic food credits for four months, worth 1 million tomans--about
$7 when the program was announced--the payments were rapidly eroded by
inflation and the rial's continuing collapse.

At the start of the calendar year, the country's minimum wage rose to 10
million tomans per month, equivalent at the time to $100. But with the
outbreak of the war and a rise in the dollar exchange rate, the minimum wage
by September had once again fallen to the equivalent of $80--even as the price
of food rose 3.6% in August alone and stood approximately 128% higher than a
year earlier.

According to Consumer Price Index (CPI) reports published by Iran's
Statistical Center, which measure the price of a basket of basic items for
each household, prices for basic goods are 2.7 times higher than two years
ago, while wages have not moved or have even declined.

"Before, even buying small quantities of fruit was a source of embarrassment,
and people would feel ashamed, for example, to buy half a kilo of something.
But now, even buying fruit one piece at a time is no longer something to be
ashamed of. People simply don't have the money to spend, and those who have
children or a pregnant wife cannot cut fresh fruit and vegetables from their
shopping list," said a 35-year-old resident of Tehran. "I'm not even talking
about expenses like entertainment or going to restaurants. Ordinary household
shopping alone eats up an average salary. The reason you walk around the city
and see everyone angry and arguing with each other is this situation. People
see that they are constantly working, but every day they are getting poorer.
These things put a lot of pressure on people's nerves."

Even though many people have cut parts of their diets, such as protein, dairy
products, or fresh vegetables, because of economic pressures, the financial
burden of rising medical prices continues to weigh on them.

Sanctions and the naval blockade, which have prevented raw materials needed
for the production of medicines from entering Iran--along with the destruction
of a large number of pharmaceutical manufacturing plants during the war--have
had a significant impact both on the availability of medicines and on their
cost.

"The increase in the price of raw materials, the inability to secure foreign
currency, and other economic problems have caused medicine prices to rise and
production to decline. On the other hand, because pharmacists cannot adjust
their selling prices in line with their costs, it costs them more to produce
the medicines than they can sell them for, putting them under even greater
pressure, which also affects the market," Dr. Shahram Kalantari, head of the
Iranian Pharmacists Association, told the Mehr news agency. "All of this is
happening while the government is unable to properly repay its debts to
pharmacists and pharmacies, placing them under even greater economic
pressure."

The prices of basic painkillers like ibuprofen and antibiotics like
amoxicillin have doubled or tripled over the past year, leaving many Iranians
in a constant struggle to track down lifesaving medicines which are normally
widely available.

"Poverty in Iran has been increasing," said Javad Hoseini, the head of Iran's
State Welfare Organization, according to ILNA, the Iranian labor news agency.
"And today the population living below the absolute poverty line has risen
from 16 million to 34 million people, while people's economic resilience has
declined and Iran is facing the widespread nature of poverty."

That estimate came just weeks before the second wave of U.S. attacks, and
before the new U.S. blockade and economic sanctions campaign that have raised
the level of economic warfare against Iranians to an unprecedented level.

## Buy Now, Pay Later

In the absence of a functional economy where individuals can use their wages
to purchase the goods they need, Iran has seen an explosion of short-term
personal loan programs, referred to as "Buy Now, Pay Later" services, where
individuals can use debt to finance the purchase of clothing, food, and small
consumer goods.

An online women's clothing store that operates on Instagram launched its own
loan service just two months after the most recent war began, citing what the
store itself described as "numerous customer requests."

Yet even this stopgap measure has done little to keep the gears of the economy
turning, as low cash liquidity in an economy increasingly running on debt and
deferred payments means retailers lack the money to replenish their
inventories. This summer, Iran's Purchasing Managers Index, known as the
Shamkh, showed
[contracting](https://tejaratnews.com/%D8%A8%D9%87%D8%A8%D9%88%D8%AF-%D8%B4%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AE-%D8%A7%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%AF-%D8%AF%D8%B1-%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B1%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%87-%D8%AA%D9%88%D9%84%DB%8C%D8%AF-%D8%AC%D8%A7%D9%86)
net figures for new orders, inventories, sales, and exports for the 16th
consecutive month.

"The economic situation has become such that people genuinely need installment
plans even to buy ordinary clothes for themselves. But the problem with buy-
now-pay-later services is that they make it harder for us to buy and replace
our raw materials," said the manager of a clothing store. "On the other hand,
if we refuse to offer these services, our sales will decline. Selling the
products and hoping that the money comes back is better than keeping the goods
in storage and waiting for people's economic situation to improve."

While some U.S. officials initially framed the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran as an
effort to liberate Iranians from authoritarian rule, the subsequent sanctions
campaign and blockade have been bluntly described as a means of destroying
Iranian society by deepening economic deprivation and provoking domestic
unrest.

"We have the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in
history," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
[said](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/20/bessent-economy-iran-war-trump.html) in
August, adding: "We are going to collapse this regime." Earlier, Bessent
[told](https://www.britt.senate.gov/news/press-releases/u-s-senator-katie-
britt-questions-treasury-secretary-scott-bessent-during-senate-banking-
hearing/) the Senate Banking Committee that Washington had "created a dollar
shortage" in Iran, sending its currency into freefall and causing inflation to
explode--"and hence we have seen the Iranian people out on the street."

Iran's total trade has fallen by an estimated 25-35%, with imports declining
faster than exports, while the workforce has dropped by about 450,000 from a
year earlier, according to figures provided by the Iranian government. The
International Monetary Fund forecasts that the economy will contract by 6.1%
in 2026, as inflation drives up business expenses and consumers cut back their
own spending, including on food and basic household goods.

While the U.S. sanctions are succeeding in causing the impoverishment of
Iranians, there is little indication that they are set to trigger an uprising
that would deliver victory in the U.S. campaign.

Many Iranians who spoke to Drop Site said that their concerns had shifted to
merely surviving rather than pursuing political change or confronting a
government that has intensified its hold on society amid the war.

"I can see with my own eyes that despite having a steady income--or sometimes
even earning more money than I did in some previous months--I am getting
poorer every day. When I go to a cafe, I have to go through the entire menu
and choose the cheapest thing available. Even that cheapest option gets more
expensive every day," said a 27-year-old student living in the city of Karaj.
"Our lives weren't like this before. We didn't have to count every penny and
calculate every expense. Like many others, I have turned to credit-payment
services and installment purchases because I cannot afford the cost of living.
A pair of sneakers costs the equivalent of one month's salary for a person in
Tehran, and the 'buy now, pay later' services even exist for buying food,
which shows just how bad people's economic situation has become. In such
circumstances, it is obvious that everyone's focus just shifts toward
survival."

## Rising Inequality

At the same time that the Trump administration announced its Economic Outcast
program against Iran, Iranian government spokesperson Fatima Mohajerani,
[responding](https://donya-e-
eqtesad.com/%D8%A8%D8%AE%D8%B4-%D8%B3%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AA-%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86-62/4291026-%D9%85%D9%87%D8%A7%D8%AC%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86%DB%8C-%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%B4%D8%A7%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D8%B7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%85%DB%8C%D8%B2%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%82%D8%B1-%D9%85%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%85-%D9%86%DB%8C%D8%A7%D8%B2-%D8%A8%D9%87-%D9%85%D8%AC%D9%88%D8%B2-%D8%B4%D9%88%D8%B1%D8%A7%DB%8C-%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%84%DB%8C-%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%86%DB%8C%D8%AA-%D9%85%D9%84%DB%8C-%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%AF-%D9%81%DB%8C%D9%84%D9%85)
to a question about poverty rates in Iran in late August, told reporters: "The
publication of statistics and figures related to the issue of poverty is
subject to security restrictions. Although the government has the figures and
statistics on this issue, it cannot make the numbers public."

The Iranian government's revenues are also declining day by day under the
pressure of sanctions and restrictions on oil exports caused by the blockade.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly
[claimed](https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20260825-trump-says-iran-is-not-
paying-large-segments-of-their-military/) that the Iranian government is
unable to pay the salaries of its employees and security forces, though no
such reports have emerged in Iran, and government employees and soldiers
continue reporting for work.

But a recent announcement that the government plans to
[increase](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/iran/iran-increases-gasoline-price-
heaviest-consumers-economy-struggles-rcna596518) consumer energy and gasoline
prices inside Iran--both normally subsidized by government spending--shows
clear signs that the country is under financial strain.

A large share of the expenditure items in Iran's current-year budget have been
devoted to the war, even though most of the reconstruction work for war-
related damage--estimated at between $20 billion and $40 billion, according to
Meysam Zohourian, a conservative member of the Iranian parliament--has not
even begun.

Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher
Ghalibaf, speaking publicly just days apart late last month, both warned that
the costs of running the country must somehow be covered and that the welfare
and essential needs of the population cannot be postponed indefinitely.

"No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do
not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we
will not endure," said Ghalibaf on August 21. Days later, Pezeshkian echoed
his sentiments with apparent frustration, stating, "Some say sanctions have no
effect at all. I really don't know what to say to those people."

Their remarks were directed at domestic hardliners who made demands for major
upfront sanctions relief and reparations a condition for negotiations, as well
as other segments of the Iranian establishment alleged to be opposed to talks
entirely. But the comments have also fueled speculation about the government's
concerns over how much economic pressure the population can withstand.

At the same time, amid growing deprivation, the display of excesses such as
wrapping red meat in bacon, or cafes serving caviar for breakfast has
heightened the sense of inequality in Iran. In the comments section of an
Instagram post showing the preparation of a meat dish, one user wrote: "Eating
something like this even once has become a dream for me," while another added:
"I hold the country's officials responsible for this situation."
